original_question: Let Γ and ∆ be residually soluble groups and let ψ: Γ -> ∆ be a homomorphism such that the induced map on true prosoluble completions PS(ψ): PS(Γ) -> PS(∆) is an isomorphism. Determine how far ψ can fail to be an isomorphism, and in particular what additional hypotheses on Γ and ∆, such as finite generation or finite presentation, force ψ itself to be an isomorphism.
target_in_paper: Introduction, item (i): the prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck's problem for true prosoluble completions.
correct_elements: The draft already captures the paper's main open problem very closely: it uses residually soluble groups Gamma and Delta, a homomorphism psi: Gamma -> Delta, the hypothesis that the induced map on true prosoluble completions PS(psi): PS(Gamma) -> PS(Delta) is an isomorphism, and it asks exactly how far psi can be from an isomorphism and whether extra finiteness assumptions such as finite generation or finite presentation force psi to be an isomorphism.
missing_details: The paper frames this explicitly as an open problem, not as a solved theorem, so 'determine' is stronger than the paper's intent; a paper-faithful version should ask 'how far can psi fail to be an isomorphism?' or 'under what hypotheses must psi be an isomorphism?'.
To be stand-alone, the question should define PS(G) as the true prosoluble completion, i.e. the inverse limit over all soluble quotients G/N with N normal in G.
It should make clear that 'true prosoluble completion' is the paper's PS(G), which is distinct from the more standard prosoluble completion built only from finite soluble quotients.
If one uses the derived-series reformulation, one must define D_0(G)=G and D_{j+1}(G)=[D_j(G),D_j(G)], and specify the quantifier 'for every j >= 1'.

The draft does not mention the paper's later sharpened special case in which the domain is a finitely generated free group and the codomain is residually soluble but not free; this is the concrete unresolved test case emphasized in Section 7.C.

The draft does not note the nuance from Section 7.C that abstract isomorphisms of the derived-series quotients are weaker than asking for a single homomorphism psi that induces all those isomorphisms simultaneously.
refined_question: Prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck's problem: let Gamma and Delta be residually soluble groups, and let psi: Gamma -> Delta be a homomorphism such that the induced map on true prosoluble completions PS(psi): PS(Gamma) -> PS(Delta) is an isomorphism, where PS(G)=lim_{N normal in G, G/N soluble} G/N. How far can psi fail to be an isomorphism? In particular, which additional hypotheses on Gamma and Delta, such as finite generation or finite presentation, are sufficient to force psi itself to be an isomorphism?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, writing D_0(G)=G and D_{j+1}(G)=[D_j(G),D_j(G)], ask for homomorphisms psi: Gamma -> Delta between residually soluble groups that induce isomorphisms Gamma/D_j(Gamma) -> Delta/D_j(Delta) for every j >= 1; under what extra hypotheses must psi be an isomorphism?
justification: The draft is essentially a near-verbatim restatement of Introduction item (i), which the authors single out as their main prosoluble analogue of Grothendieck's problem. I kept that broader formulation rather than replacing it by the narrower free-group question in Section 7.C, because Section 7.C is presented as a later special case and test problem, not as the primary statement. The derived-series alternate formulation is paper-faithful because Sections 5.B-5.D identify PS(G) with the completion defined by the ordinary derived series and compare the quotients PS(G)/D_j(PS(G)) with G/D_j(G).
